Most people think it is intellect that makes 
a great scientist . They are wrong, it is 
character . —Albert Einstein 

Character is the thing that distinguishes a 
good scout from a bad one, 

— The first Official boy Scout 
Handbook, 1911 

What is character? 

Character is an elusive, but increasingly 
important concept. Aristocrats and 
royalty seem to have it, better schools try 
to develop it, we all wish we had more of 
it, but no one seems sure what it really is. 

The Oxford Dictionary defines 
“character” as “the sum of the moral and 
mental qualities which distinguish an 
individual”. The Oxford American 
defines it as “all those qualities that make 
a person what he is and different from 
others”. 

Character has to do with who we are. It 
is a synergistic blend of attributes like 
initiative, courage, commitment, and 
resourcefulness. It is the way an individual 
orchestrates and applies skills, knowledge, 
attitudes and experience to the problems 
and opportunities of daily living. 
Character is the essence of our individu¬ 
ality and excellence. It determines who we 
will become. 


“Character is the sum of a person’s 
powers, their nature as a being. Power 
is used here in its broadest sense, and 
means all of the abilities of an organism 
to change itself or the environment. 
Most human powers are either learned 
or may be enhanced, modified or 
directed by learning. Attributes of 
character are expressed as “high order 
skill”, abilities such as courage, cheer¬ 
fulness, compassion, resilience, 
creativity or initiative. High order 
skills are general powers that are useful 
in a wide range of different situations. 
Literacy is a high order skill, as are 
artistry, ingenuity and mechanical 
“savvy”. There are hundreds of high 
order skills that could make up 
character. The problem for any society 
is deciding which powers to en¬ 
courage.” (Low, 1985)* 

Each age, or era, has its own problems 
and opportunities. Different specific skills 
and powers are needed to respond 
effectively to the challenges posed by the 
events and circumstances of different 
eras. Rugged individualism and ruthless 
industrialism gave way to corporate 
gamesmen and “the man in the grey 
flannel suit.” The organization man is 
now giving way to information brokers, 
entrepreneurs, intrapreneurs and 
innovators. Different times and different 
circumstances require different attributes 
of character. 

The present age is one of change and 
complexity. It is a time of diversity and 
options, a time of both danger and 
opportunity. It is a time of great freedom 
which requires the wise use of personal 
freedom. Indeed, character is nothing less 
than the ability to make use of freedom. It 
is the ability to take advantage of freedom 
from restraint but, more important, 
character empowers us to be free to act. A 
well developed character enables us to 
choose from among the choices, to initiate 
action, to turn dreams into reality and to 
take personal responsibility for who we — 
and our world — become. 

Character involves a sense of 
“response-ability” — the ability to 
respond — made possible, and necessary, 
by the increasing and sometimes 
frightening erosion of the power of 
external structures which, traditionally, 
have provided guidance and direction for 
individuals and groups. 


Why do we need to develop character? 

Our world, our society — and with 
them our traditional approaches to 
human growth, learning and develop¬ 
ment — have been changing so rapidly 
that our cultural supports are crumbling. 
We now have to consciously design things 
— machines, systems, procedures, 
solutions to professional and personal 
problems — that we have never had to 
think about before. 

In the face of increasing complexity and 
rapidly escalating change, each of us must 
develop our own powers, engage the 
culture and environment with those 
powers and, in the process, create and 
continuously re-create who we become. 
We can no longer rely only on traditional 
approaches to learning and growth to 
develop the abilities we need to manage 
ourselves and our environments. We are, 
each of us, responsible for our own 
powers, our own becoming. 

Our schools do not develop the high 
order skills we need to meet and manage 
complex, changing conditions. The 
images of the mass media are ineffective 
at best and harmful at worst as models of 
general powers and high order skills. 
Family, church and community are less 
effective today than in simpler, more 
stable times. Yet, we desperately need 
individuals who can translate ideas into 
action, who can learn from their own 
experience, who understand how and why 
to take part in the culture that sustains 
them and who know how, and why, to 
take charge of their own lives and lead 
themselves into the future. 

“Parents, educators and counsellors, 
are faced with a difficult challenge. 
Our culture is in a difficult “in be¬ 
tween” stage in its approaches to 
human development. We still rely on 
many traditional methods of sociali¬ 
zation to produce acceptable be¬ 
haviour by encouraging conformity, 
while at the same time recognizing the 
need for greater levels of responsible 
autonomy and self-direction. We also 
know that the schools cannot carry the 
whole burden of youth development, 
but do not yet know what other kinds 
of arrangements should be in place, 
who should do what, and how the 
whole thing ties together.” (Low 1985)* 


26 



What does character have to do with 
camp? 

Waiting for schools and teachers to 
develop new approaches and arrange¬ 
ments for human development and 
personal growth is like hoping railroaders 
will develop new forms of air travel. Not 
likely. Schools have enough trouble trying 
to teach the 3 R’s without having to worry 
about the basics of character develop¬ 
ment. Character development is based on 
a different set of basics — the 3 W’s: 
Will, Wisdom and Wherewithal — 
which correspond to the generative skills 
of self-motivation, self-management and 
self-mastery. It is the development of 
these skills that requires new 
arrangements and new approaches. 

To ensure the development of basic 
character skills we will have to break out 
of our narrow, categorical thinking that 
learning and growth take place only in 
formal educational settings like schools. 
We will have to look to other areas of 
human life for answers. If we look 
carefully we will discover that the better 
experiential learning and recreation 
programs are already encouraging and 
facilitating the growth of these skills. One 
area that holds great promise is the 
camping movement. The basic character 
skills are developed more by a summer at 
camp than they are by a year in most 
schools. 

Good summer camps have always, 
implicitly or explicitly, contributed to the 
development of personal powers and 
character. Young people — both campers 
and counsellors — become engaged with 
an environment ideally suited for 
developing high order skills and testing 
personal powers. That engagement 
increases a learner’s ability to do things, 
to handle change and stress, and to take 
responsibility for actions and experience. 
And with those skills and insights comes a 
sense that he or she “can do”. And do 
better. Confidence and competence 
increase. A sense of excellence and 
responsibility are born. 

Camping offers opportunities for 
learning in a variety of areas from 
physical skills to crafts to social skills. It 
provides a chance to get away from the 
routine of home and school, to try out 
new ways of acting and being. It demands 
responsibility, particularly from young 
leaders. (In fact, there is probably no 
other environment in which young people 
are trusted so highly or offered so much 
responsibility than that of counselling 
children at camp.) Camp offers training, 
coaching, counselling, and peer-learning. 
It provides immediate feedback and 
correction without the stigma of grades 
and ranking. It allows young people to 
make mistakes and learn from them — 
a skill we are discovering is critical for 
peak performance in personal and pro¬ 
fessional life throughout life. Camp 


encourages integrated learning and 
growth, perhaps more than any other 
social institution we have. And it does so 
without much ado about the process, so 
learning happens naturally, effortlessly 
and enjoyaably. 

Camp is an empowering environment. 
It is an excellent testing ground for the 
development of character. Character 
development is already implicit in many of 
the approaches and programs which can 
be found in any good camp. But, we can 
do more. We can build on what exists to 
make character development an explicit 
part of the camping process. We can make 
the development of personal powers, and 
an understanding of the ways those 
powers are used, a valued goal of the 
camping experience. Making explicit the 
principles and process by which character 
is developed will make it possible to 
ensure that camping’s full potential can be 
used to encourage young people to 
develop general skills, broad powers and 
power over those powers. 

What does character have to do with 
leadership? 

Developing character is an act of em¬ 
powerment. Power is “the ability to do 
something”. It is the basic energy of 
human achievement, the capacity to 
initiate and carry out action, the ability to 
translate intention into reality and sustain 
it. Empowerment — the evolution of 
character — involves developing specific 
powers, and power over those powers. 
Persons of character use power wisely. 
They are just as interested in “know- 
why” as they are in “know-how”. They 
are concerned about doing the right thing 
more than they are about doing things 
right. They are leaders — of others, 
sometimes — but always of themselves. 

Leadership for character development 
is different than “I lead, you follow’’ 
leadership. Beyond a basic level the 
developing character is a self-led process. 
Therefore, the leadership approach that 
best facilitates its development is an 
empowering self-leadership process, one 
which transforms followers into leaders. 
Equipping camp staff and counsellors 
with the skills, strategies and principles of 
self-leadership will ensure an under¬ 
standing of the processes by which 
character is developed. It will enable them 
to facilitate that process more effectively 
and, indeed, if desired, to design and 
develop programs that make the 
development of character their primary 
goal. It will also enable them to empower 
themselves. 

There are two key elements in leader¬ 
ship for character development — the 
leaders and the environment — and both 
can be developed to ensure that they 
contribute effectively to the 
empowerment and growth of our young 
people. 


Four aspects of effective leadership 
stand out. Leaders have a sense of vision. 
They know what they want to achieve, 
they know what they believe in. They have 
a purpose, a mission that motivates them, 
which attracts and pulls their followers. 

Good leaders are effective communi¬ 
cators. Specifically they are good at 
sharing their vision in such a way that it 
induces enthusiasm in others and commit¬ 
ment to an important purpose. 

Good leaders “walk their talk”. By 
constantly and clearly practicing what 
they preach, good leaders engender the 
trust necessary to implement their vision. 

Finally, good leaders know that self- 
empowerment is essential. They know 
that the best way to transform, or 
improve, or empower others is, first, 
empower yourself. Warren Bennis, on 
whose research these elements of 
leadership are based, says, “Management 
of self is critical. Without it leaders may 
do more harm than good”.** Good 
leaders work at developing their own self- 
regard by developing and improving their 
skills, and aligning their purpose and 
goals with the needs of the organization. 
They are also positive thinkers, able to see 
problems as challenges, to learn from 
mistakes or setbacks, and look ahead to 
opportunity with enthusiasm and energy. 
High self regard and a positive attitude are 
contagious. And they are empowering. 
Not only of leaders, but also those who 
follow them. 

Empowering environments have four 
essential components as well. The first is 
significance. To be empowering, events 
and circumstances must be important, 
even momentous. They must have 
personal meaning for campers. 

The second component of empower¬ 
ment is competence. Campers must have a 
sense that they are learning new things, 
mastering new skills, developing their 
powers. 

A sense of community is essential. 
Sharing common purpose, working and 
playing together is empowering. Camps 
are almost unique in the degree of 
community they foster. 

Finally, enjoyment, or plain old fun, is 
a critical element in empowerment. Fun is 
motivating, it enhances learning and is 
rewarding in itself. 

Taking part in enjoyable, meaningful 
activities, building personal and 
interpersonal skills with a group of new 
friends under the watchful eye of a 
confident, trusted leader who cares 
deeply, who listens carefully, and gives 
you good advice when it is needed — 
isn’t that what camp is all about? 

When you have leaders with the 
qualities described above working in 
environments containing the basics of 
empowerment, great things happen. 


27 




Young people grow and learn, they 
develop skills and powers. And they 
develop the character they will need to be 
able to make good and wise use of those 
powers in years to come. 

A Challenge for Camping 

The development of character and 
excellence — the facilitation of personal 
powers and individual becoming — is one 
of the highest goals any institution or 
organization can aspire to. Few of our 
traditional institutions are ready or willing 
to undertake this important task. Most of 
them lack the kind of open, challenging 
environment necessary to carry it out. 
Camps are ideally suited for this 
challenge. 

Camp — and other outdoor and 
experiential education programs — is a 
natural place to empower individuals and 
enhance their character. By under¬ 
standing the importance of character and 
applying the basic principles of 
empowerment the camping movement can 
quietly and unassumingly transform itself 
into a leader in the development of 
character — on the cutting edge of 
human growth and development — 
without losing the naturalness, the 
spontaneity and the closeness that makes 
camp unique. 

Our society is in a difficult transition. 
Old ways do not work, new ways have yet 


to be invented. It will take all we can do to 
successfully navigate through the tides of 
change which threaten to capsize us. We 
can no longer afford to trust monolithic 
institutions such as schools and govern¬ 
ments to care for us and for our develop¬ 
ment. It is up to all of us — in any and all 
the ways we can — to take charge of our 
lives, our learning and our growth. It is up 
to us to lead ourselves. And to equip our 
children to lead themselves. Self¬ 
leadership is the basis of all effective 
leadership. It is a critical factor in whether 
or not we make it through these changing 
times successfully. 

The absence of ineffectiveness of 
leadership implies the absence of 
vision, a dreamless society, and this 
will result, at best in the maintenance 
of the status quo or, at worst, in the 
disintegration of our society because 
of lack of purpose and cohesion. 

Warren Bennis in Leaders. 

This, then, is the challenge — em¬ 
powering our youth to create their own 
vision, take charge of their own develop¬ 
ment, shape their own character and start 
on a path toward excellence. It is a 
challenge worthy of the best of us. 
Nothing less than the continued stability 
and flourishing of our selves and our 
world is at stake. Could there be a more 
appropriate and exciting challenge for the 
camping movement? Could there be a 


more empowering vision for us all as we 
head toward the 21st Century? 


* References attributed to Ken Low 
from unpublished briefing papers pre¬ 
pared for the Action Studies Institute. 

** Warren Bennis’s research is detailed in 
Leaders , by Warren Bennis and Burt 
Namus, Harper and Row, 1985. 



UNDER OPEN SKIES 

A CAMPER S PRAYER 

God of the open air, we rejoice that we can live in touch with 
sunshine and rain and growing things. The drum-beat of a 
shower on the tent roof, the fragrance of fresh, cool forest trails, 
an evening under the stars all speak to us of You. No one but you 
could ever supply such beauty. No one but You could ever 
provide the inner strength which comes from sleeping under the 
stars, or singing together around a campfire, or paddling down a 
sleepy river. We feel we must absorb every bit of joy and 
companionship that comes from life together in the open. 

The trees stand tall and straight above us, and we feel that we 
want to grow to be like them. The wind sings in the trees, and we 
try to remember that sound forever. The stars sparkle in a dark 
night sky, and we fall asleep wondering. Oh God, keep us good 
campers, we pray . . . throughout all our lives . . . striving to 
uphold all that is pure and ideal. God of the open air, this is our 
prayer today. AMEN. 

A BENEDICTION 

May the Silence of the hills, 

The Joy of the wind, 

The Music of the birds, 

The Fire of the sun, 

The strength of the trees, 

And the Faith of youth, 

In all of which is God, 

Be in our hearts 
Now and evermore. 


submitted by Madelene Allen 
Camp Ouareau, St. Donat, Quebec 

A prayer adapted from the Cub-Scout Prayer by 
Catherine Marshall (p. 36. God Loves You.) 

Dear Father, this is Joan talking. 

Of course You know 
I’m at camp. 

I’ve tried to be good today — 
and I sure am having a good time. 

Swimming and paddling that canoe, 
and going fishing are such fun. 

Tm glad You thought of making cool blue water, 
and sunshine and silvery fish. 

But, God, what about that fish that got away yesterday? 
Where did he go? 

You make such pretty things, God. 

I like the way the pine trees stand up on the hill. 

I like the red of the flash of the wing of the red-winged 
blackbird, 

the funny feel of the milkweed pod I picked, 
the big, golden moon, 

and the feel of wiggling my toes in the cool, wet sand. 

Thank you God for making all these things. 

Oh . . . and please bless Mom and Dad and my friends and 
my counsellor, and help me be a good camper all day today. 
Good Morning God.

ENVIRONMENTAL PROGRAMS 


PROGRAMS TO USE ON THE MOVE 

by Jean Funk 

Chairman of the Environmental Concerns Committee ofC. C.A. 


Les Programmes en marche 

Les chasses suivantes peuvent etre utilises par un 
conseiller en route des activites, aux promenades et aux 
voyages k canot... ou seui comme activite speciale de la 
nature. Principalement, ces chasses sont pour les enfant 
ag6sde6&12 ans. 

The following hunts can be used by a counsellor while going to 
program activities ; on day hikes and canoe trips... or as a special 
nature activity in themselves . These are primarily for 6-12 year 
olds . 


THIRTY-SECOND FIELD TRIP 

Are you looking for an outdoor winter activity which will 
neither numb the brain, freeze the fingers, nor cause hypo¬ 
thermia? Weil, here it is! After defining boundaries, send partici¬ 
pants out individually, in pairs, or in groups to find (but not 
bring back) examples of the things below. You may choose to 
give them each item individually or a list of several to be found 
within a certain time limit. You may wish to choose only items 
which are related to your particular theme of study (such as 
‘change’, ‘homes’ or ‘communities’). Results may be discussed 
orally or recorded on a worksheet. 


YOU HAVE THIRTY SECONDS TO FIND: 

a) something that is smooth 

b) something that is rough 

c) a living thing 

d) a dead thing 

e) a source of food 

f) something that is brown 

g) something whose name starts with the letter ‘D’ 

h) something that has three or more syllables in its name 

i) a type of shelter 

j) the most common color 

k) something that is circular 

l) something that is really neat 

m) the oldest thing 

n) the youngest thing 

o) two things that are alike 

p) the tallest thing 

r) something that is changing 

s) something that is more than two colors 

t) something that is moist 

u) something that has a strong smell 

v) the loudest sound you hear 

w) something you dislike 

x) something that is hard 

y) something that is soft 

z) your favorite thing 


PLANT SCAVENGER HUNT 

Scavenger hunts are a useful tool to capture and focus interest 
on specific natural objects. This particular activity is an opening 
activity to create an awareness of the diversity of plants and plant 
happenings. 

Materials 

Copies of the “Plant Scavenger Hunt” Sheet 

Plastic bags 

Pencils 

Magnifiers 

Optional: One or more prizes for winning teams (If possible, 

the prizes should be related to plants; e.g., fruit, 
something made of wood, or handicrafts made 
from plants). 

Location 

In a wooded area or field 
Outdoor Activity 

1. Have participants assemble in small teams. Explain the 
ground rules of the scavenger hunt paying particular 
attention to safety concerns such as boundaries, staying 
with one’s team and returning on an agreed upon signal 
(e.g., whistle blowing). 

2. Establish a time limit (perhaps a half hour) and let the 
participants begin their search. 

3. Check off each item for the first team back and see if they 
have all the items, let these participants help in judging 
the other teams coming in. 

4. When the time is up have all the teams sit in one large 
circle and share the items one by one. 

5. Where items are particularly interesting encourage children 
to ask questions and speculate on the answers. 

6. Save all items for later work, or return items back to the 
natural environment. 

Follow-up Activities 

1. Have participants sort the scavenger hunt items into groups 
such as the following: 

— interesting shapes or patterns 

— interesting smells 

— interesting colors 

— interesting to touch 

— seeds 

— insect homes or food 

— foods for mammals 

2. Have groups of participants make posters promoting 
diversity and/or bulletin board displays from the items 
collected. 

3. Do a follow-up study on one or more of the display 
topics: seeds, insect homes or food for wild creatures. 

4. As an alternate activity have participants make a village or 
collage-poem or collage-story using the items they brought 
back.

A NATURE HUNT 


MASTER LIST: DO NOT CUT 


Purpose: A fun way to explore a new area. It’s also a great 

“quiet down and explore” activity for a very 
active day. 


MASTER LIST: DO NOT CUT 

** Please do not pick, harm or remove any piece of anything that 
is still alive. 

1. Bring back something you can see light through. 

2. Bring back something to make music with. 

3. Bring back a soft rock. 

4. Bring back something gooey (use container provided). 

5. Find three things that have changed — 

since this morning... 
since last winter... 
since you were bom... 

Tell us about them 

6. Find and draw a picture of something that is ending its 
life and something that is beginning its life. 

7. Bring back the sound of the rain (even if it isn’t raining 
right now). 

8. Find something natural to mark with. Bring back a picture 
you drew with it. 

9. Find 3 signs that animals are living here. What animals 
do you think they are? List them. 

10. Describe something that changes so slowly that you don’t 
notice. 

11. Draw the wind. 

12. Bring back a piece of litter — write a story about its life. 
What would happen to it if you left it where you found it? 

13. Measure and record the length of the shadow of the tallest 
person in your group, using a finger, toe, hand, foot, arm 
or leg as a ruler. 

14. Find something you would like to make better. Describe 
how ydu would improve it. 

15. Using everyone in your group, make a human sculpture to 
show the other groups something that you saw on your 
hike. 

16. Bring back rubbings of 3 different textures. Place an object 
(eg. a piece of bark) under your paper, then run your 
crayon over the paper. This will be your rubbing. Tell us 
where you got your rubbing from. 

17. Draw a picture with 5 different colours you see. 

18. Find something that you don’t understand and make up a 
question about it to ask the others. 

19. List 10 words to describe a natural object 10 paces to your 
left. 

20. Find, then draw or describe a sign of the season.

Purpose: To stimulate participants to question the things 

they observe about them, especially out-of- 
doors. 


Activity Divide the children into groups and have them 
Description: find the item or find examples of the list from 
both land and water. 


Follow-up A quiet-down activity after the hunt can be a 
Activity: discussion of how these “treasures” are inter¬ 

related (food chains or webs).

— three oxygen-takers

— a camouflaged animal; one that can hide 
well in its surroundings 

— an important food smaller than your 
fingernail

THE QUESTION HUNT* 

To stimulate children to question the things they 
perceive about them, especially out-of-doors. 

You’ve decided to introduce a group of partici¬ 
pants to a variety of ‘habitats’. 

Your prime concern is to initiate QUESTIONING 
and to put the load of activity and the responsi¬ 
bility for answering questions on the shoulders 
of the whole group. 

(1) Having selected three or four suitable sites in 
advance of the exercise, take the group to 
the first area. 

(2) Explain to the group that each person will 
have 3 - 5 minutes to search the immediate 
area to come up with a question to be shared 
with the group. 

(3) When the area has been searched, gather the 
group together and have each person give 
their question . . . but insist that no answers 
be given. The leader should also have a 
question (hopefully a provocative one that 
leaves the group curious). 

(4) Go to the second site; repeat the activity, 
but this time after all the questions have 
been given, ask for answers to any of the 
questions posed (but notably not trying to 
come up with answers to all the questions). 

(5) The activity can be extended by having: 

i) an easy and a hard question at subse¬ 
quent sites, or 

ii) having the participants prepare a 
written list of questions at a later site, or 

iii) having teams compose questions to¬ 
gether to initiate some sharing and 
teamwork. 

(1) You will have initiated the questioning pro¬ 
cess. 

(2) You will have established that answers are 
neither expected nor necessary for every 
question. 

(3) The participants will have felt accomplish¬ 
ment at asking questions as opposed to being 
afraid to show their ignorance. 

(4) You will have some feeling for the com¬ 
petence of your group members and may be 
able to assign some participants to be 
‘experts’ in certain areas. If nothing else, 
the expert might simply be designated by 
virtue of carrying the appropriate identifi¬ 
cation guide or field manual. 


♦Adapted from “Alberta Environment”

SUBSCRIPTION INFORMATION 

Canadian Camping Magazine is the official publication of the Canadian Camping Association. 
Editorial offices of the Magazine are located at R.R. #1, Huntsville, Ontario, P0A 1K0. 

Membership in the C.C.A., as a result of membership in a provincial camping association, 
includes a subscription to the Magazine. Non member subscription is $8.00/year. Single issue price 
is $2.00. Make cheques payable to the Canadian Camping Association. Send subscriptions, sub - 
missions, or address changes to the editorial offices. 

Canadian Camping Magazine is published four times yearly. Deadlines for submissions are 
October 1, December 1, February 15 and May I. Material in Canadian Camping Magazine may 
not be reproduced in any form without the expressed written permission of the editor. Copyright 
1986 Canadian Camping Association.

COVER 

The cover photo of the Washington Monument was taken in 
Washington, D.C. at the Second International Camping 
Congress. The theme of the Congress was ‘Our Fragile World*. 

LA COUVERTURE 

La photo illustree en couverture du monument de Washington 
irent du deuxieme “International Camping Congress” & 
Washington, D.C. Le theme du Congres etait “Notre monde 
fragile”.
